raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man, who was a former smoker and had chronic silicosis caused by 14 years of work in the granite industry, was admitted to the hospital after an episode of hemoptysis. The amount of blood expectorated was estimated at more than 200 mL. He also had a one-month history of productive cough with blood in the sputum. He had previous history of tuberculosis, with the last episode approximately two years prior, when he received isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide for two months, followed by four months of isoniazid and rifampin. He had been asymptomatic since then.
On physical examination, the patient was emaciated and pale. His blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, his pulse was 104 beats/min, and his respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min. Lung auscultation revealed rhonchi and wheezing in both lungs. No other alterations were seen in the physical examination. A blood chemistry screening was normal, including negative finding by anti-HIV. Immunodiffusion tests were negative for Aspergillus.
A chest radiograph (Figure 1) and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the thorax (Figure 2) showed bilateral conglomerate masses, one with cavitation, associated with multiple small nodules, in addition to calcifications of the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, paracicatricial emphysema, architectural distortion, and enlargement of the central pulmonary arteries. No other parenchymal findings were suggestive of active tuberculosis.
The expectorated sputum was negative for acid-fast bacilli and the patient underwent a bronchoscopy that showed evidence of active bleeding. Direct examination of the bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for tuberculosis, fungi, or malignancy. Culturing was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and negative for fungi.
Because of the enlarged pulmonary arteries, Doppler ecocardiography was performed, showing left ventricular diastolic function, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary arterial hypertension with a systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mmHg. The patient underwent an angiogram of the common bronchial trunk that showed marked hypervascularity and enlargement of left bronchial artery, which was selectively catheterized and subsequently embolized with polyvinyl alcohol particles (PVA). Bleeding stopped after embolization. The patient was treated for tuberculosis with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for two months, followed by seven months of isoniazid and rifampin. After the embolization and clinical treatment for tuberculosis, the patient progressed well, with improvement in his respiratory symptoms, and no rebleeding after a follow-up of two years.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male former granite worker with chronic silicosis presented with massive hemoptysis (>200 mL) following a 1-month history of blood-streaked productive cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a 1-month history of productive cough with blood-streaked sputum that culminated in an episode of massive hemoptysis (>200 mL) prompting hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic silicosis from 14 years of work in the granite industry; former smoker; pulmonary tuberculosis treated 2 years prior with a 6-month regimen (2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin), asymptomatic until 1 month prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for productive cough with blood-streaked sputum for 1 month and acute massive hemoptysis (>200 mL).

objective.physical_examination: Emaciated and pale; blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, pulse 104 bpm, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral rhonchi and wheezing; remainder of the physical exam was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood chemistry panel and anti-HIV serology were normal/negative. Expectorated sputum AFB smear was negative. Chest radiograph showed bilateral conglomerate masses (one cavitary), multiple small nodules, calcified hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes, and enlarged central pulmonary arteries. Doppler echocardiography demonstrated left ventricular diastolic dysfunction, mild tricuspid regurgitation, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (systolic PAP 48 mmHg).
objective.advanced_workup: Serum immunodiffusion tests for Aspergillus were negative. Thorax HRCT confirmed bilateral conglomerate masses with cavitation, multiple small silicotic nodules, hilar and mediastinal eggshell/nodal calcifications, paracicatricial emphysema, architectural distortion, and central pulmonary artery enlargement. Bronchoscopy revealed active endobronchial bleeding; BAL direct smears and fungal cultures were negative, but BAL mycobacterial culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Selective bronchial arteriography demonstrated marked hypervascularity and hypertrophy of the left bronchial artery.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Massive hemoptysis secondary to recurrent active cavitary silicotuberculosis and left bronchial artery hypervascularity in a patient with chronic silicosis and pulmonary hypertension; pulmonary aspergilloma/aspergillosis was ruled out by negative serum Aspergillus immunodiffusion and negative BAL fungal smears and cultures, and active tuberculosis was confirmed by BAL culture growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Treated with selective polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) particle embolization of the hypertrophied left bronchial artery (which immediately arrested the bleeding) followed by a 9-month anti-tuberculosis regimen (2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then 7 months of isoniazid and rifampin), achieving complete symptom resolution with no recurrent hemoptysis over 2 years of follow-up.
